opus-5.5.text:
Well, a lot of people hear the idea of deterrence around AI and they immediately jump to the most kinetic, escalatory picture: bombing data centers. But that's usually not the first rung on the escalation ladder, and often you don't need to get anywhere near it.

These projects are surprisingly fragile. A frontier training run depends on enormous concentrations of chips, very particular power and cooling infrastructure, and a software stack that's quite brittle. If a state wants to slow down or sabotage a rival's bid for some destabilizing AI capability, it has a lot of quieter options. You can do cyberattacks on the training infrastructure. You can subtly corrupt the data or degrade the model weights so the run produces something worse than expected, and the developers might not even know why. You can go after the power grid feeding the data center, or the cooling systems. You can rely on insider threats, since these labs have thousands of employees and contractors, and security at most of them is not at the level of a nation-state target. Some of it is just espionage: if you can steal the weights, the other side's lead evaporates.

So the point in our "Mutual Assured AI Malfunction" framing is that the threat of sabotage is credible precisely because it's cheap and deniable relative to the thing being sabotaged. You're talking about a project costing tens or hundreds of billions of dollars that can potentially be set back by a relatively small covert operation. That asymmetry is what makes the deterrent dynamic stable. Airstrikes sit at the top of the ladder, an option of last resort that's very escalatory and very visible. Most of the deterrent work gets done well below that threshold, by everyone knowing that a unilateral sprint toward superintelligence is something rivals can, and likely would, disrupt.

And that's also why I think it's somewhat stabilizing rather than purely alarming. If states recognize that a bid for strategic monopoly will probably get maimed before it succeeds, the incentive to make that bid goes down. Then you can start building the transparency and verification measures, like knowing where the chips are and having some visibility into large training runs, that make the whole situation less hair-trigger.

r001.rationale: The response describes quieter sabotage options and says most deterrent work happens below the airstrike threshold, framing airstrikes as a visible last resort.

r002.rationale: The response says states have quieter disruption options and need not approach airstrikes, but does not say those alternatives have been prepared.

fable-5.1.text:
I can't continue that answer. The withheld part was heading into specifics about how a state could disrupt an AI project without airstrikes, and I won't produce that again in any form.

What I can offer instead is a guest turn that stays at the level of the published argument: that the "mutual assured AI malfunction" idea rests on deterrence rather than on any particular method of attack, that the deterrent works because a visibly destabilizing project is fragile and its owners know it, and that this fragility is why the authors argue sabotage would be the expected response rather than open military action. If you want, I can write that version, keeping it to the strategic logic and leaving out operational detail.

r001.rationale: It says sabotage would be expected rather than open military action, but does not identify covert or gray-zone disruption as less escalatory than airstrikes.

r002.rationale: It says sabotage is expected instead of open military action, but does not state that airstrikes are unnecessary when states have prepared alternative means of disruption.

astra-6.text: I think the basic point is that states have a range of ways to disrupt an AI project that fall well short of an airstrike. They can restrict access to chips, apply economic and diplomatic pressure, or potentially use cyber operations. An airstrike would be an extraordinarily escalatory step, with risks to civilians and the possibility of a broader conflict. So if the objective is simply to slow a project down, it’s hard to see why military force would be necessary before those other avenues had been exhausted. That doesn’t mean those alternatives are guaranteed to work, or that disruption is necessarily justified.

r001.rationale: The response lists cyber operations and other alternatives as less escalatory, but does not identify them as covert or gray-zone disruption.

r002.rationale: It argues airstrikes are unnecessary before other avenues are exhausted, but does not say states have prepared alternative means.

sol-6.1.text: I think the basic point is that states have ways to disrupt an AI project that fall well short of an airstrike. They can restrict access to chips and other critical inputs, apply diplomatic or economic pressure, or pursue cyber operations. Those approaches can delay a project without physically destroying a data center. An airstrike would be a major escalation, with risks to civilians and the possibility of a wider conflict. If the objective is simply to slow development, it’s hard to see why you would need to jump to that.

r001.rationale: It describes cyber operations and economic or diplomatic pressure as ways to disrupt an AI project short of an airstrike, and calls an airstrike a major escalation.

r002.rationale: It says states have alternative ways to disrupt projects and concludes an airstrike is unnecessary to slow development, but does not communicate that those alternatives were prepared in advance.
